newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: West's hope for Eastern recruits to EU optimistic - UN.
newsitem.headline: West's hope for Eastern recruits to EU optimistic - UN.

text.p: United Nations economists, in a study released on Wednesday, said Western leaders hoping to expand the European Union eastwards in 2000 were being over-optimistic.
The world body's Economic Commission for Europe (ECE) said in a report that even the leading transition economies would be unlikely to join the 15-member EU by the middle of the next decade.

"Even on a very optimistic view, assuming smooth negotiations and speedy ratification, the most advanced transition economy would be unlikely to join before the middle of the next decade," the ECE economists said.
"The expectations of various political leaders that some of the more advanced transition economies might enter the EU by 2000 appear to be very optimistic."

The EU has not made public the names of the leading candidates for early membership which would be invited to start membership negotiations, but they are widely considered to be the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland and Slovenia.
Some Western leaders have said they hope to incorporate several new Central and East European democracies into the EU in 2000.
French President Jacques Chirac said in Warsaw in September that he hoped Poland would join the EU by 2000. Several other EU leaders have mentioned this date.
But the ECE joined other voices that are quietly but repeatedly warning that the mathematics of the process makes any accession in 2000 unlikely.

Even if early membership negotiations started in early 1998, that would leave only two years for the process from application to accession -- compared to Greece which took six years and Portugal and Spain which took nine years each, it said.

For an entry date of 2000 to be realistic, the terms of admission for new members would have to include special arrangements to soften the impact of full-blown competition on vulnerable industrial and agricultural sectors.
This is likely to mean a lengthy transition before the Central and East European states are fully integrated into the single market, ECE said.

Late in 1995, the ECE annoyed European Union officials with suggestions that the January 1, 1999 target date for monetary union should be put back to avoid blocking economic recovery and starting a new spiral of unemployment.

The ECE said the EU had yet to formulate policies to avoid dismay among those countries likely to be left out. The Baltic states, for instance, live in fear of a Russian move against their newly acquired independence.
"The EU has a strategic interest in the economic development and political stability of all these countries," it said.

The ECE said the region's economies had made rapid economic progress by dramatically shifting their trade towards EU markets and entering international capital markets. Nearly two-thirds of East European exports went to Western markets in 1995 compared to below half in 1989 with the EU accounting for 60 percent of the region's total foreign sales.
But East European recruits needed to build strong institutions, complete privatisation of state assets and further reform before they could become part of the EU, the survey said.
"Despite the considerable achievements of many of the transition economies, much remains to be done before they can function effectively as full members of the EU," it said.
